title: Build a personal two-pattern error log
instructions: Use Sam's eight dated review entries: (1) 3 October, editing—wrote ‘The trial was short, it produced useful observations’; feedback identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. (2) 5 October, composition—wrote ‘The survey proves every student preferred the change’ although 18 of 25 respondents preferred it. (3) 8 October, vocabulary—chose ‘ecstatic’ for a neutral school report because the rarer word seemed better. (4) 11 October, editing—wrote ‘I planned the route carefully, the rain blocked the footpath’; feedback again identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. (5) 14 October, open cloze—used one wrong preposition in a fixed expression. (6) 17 October, composition—wrote ‘This always solves the problem’ after describing one two-day trial. (7) 20 October, grammar—wrote ‘The list of materials were complete’ and then independently corrected ‘were’ to ‘was’ by finding the head subject. (8) 23 October, editing—wrote ‘The seedlings recovered, I recorded the change each evening’; feedback again identified two complete clauses joined only by a comma. Answer all six questions before viewing feedback.

parts.prompt: Which THREE entries provide evidence of one recurring sentence-boundary pattern?

options.text: Entry 1: ‘The trial was short, it produced useful observations.’
Entry 3: choosing ‘ecstatic’ for a neutral report
Entry 4: ‘I planned the route carefully, the rain blocked the footpath.’
Entry 7: ‘The list of materials were complete.’
Entry 8: ‘The seedlings recovered, I recorded the change each evening.’

choice_rationales.A: This is the first recorded comma splice between independent clauses.
choice_rationales.B: This is a register and word-choice error, not a sentence-boundary error.
choice_rationales.C: This repeats the same comma-splice structure in a later task.
choice_rationales.D: This is subject–verb agreement and was independently corrected.
choice_rationales.E: This is a third dated example of the same comma-splice structure.

parts.hint: Look for repeated structures, not merely entries that contain any grammar error.
parts.correct_explanation: Entries 1, 4 and 8 show the same observable choice across three dates: joining complete clauses with only a comma.

parts.prompt: Which label names that recurring pattern most precisely?

options.text: I am careless with punctuation.
I join two independent clauses with only a comma.
My English is weak.
I should write shorter essays.

choice_rationales.A: ‘Careless’ judges the learner but does not identify what to check.
choice_rationales.B: The label describes the repeated structure and points directly to a sentence-boundary test.
choice_rationales.C: This is too broad to guide a correction or measure improvement.
choice_rationales.D: Essay length is not the repeated fault shown by the three entries.

parts.hint: Choose a label that another reader could identify in a fresh sentence.
parts.correct_explanation: A precise error label states the observable choice rather than assigning a vague personal trait.

parts.prompt: Which should be Sam's SECOND active pattern alongside the comma splice?

options.text: Using unsupported absolute claims, shown in entries 2 and 6
Every spelling rule in English, although no spelling error appears in the log
The one incorrect preposition in entry 5, because every single error must become an active pattern
Subject–verb agreement, ignoring that entry 7 was a single error Sam independently corrected

choice_rationales.A: The pattern recurs and changes the truth and scope of the response, so it is high impact and actionable.
choice_rationales.B: A useful log is evidence-based; it cannot add an unsupported weakness.
choice_rationales.C: One recorded slip remains evidence but does not outrank the repeated, meaning-changing pattern.
choice_rationales.D: The single independently corrected example is weaker evidence of an active recurring need.

parts.hint: Balance recurrence with impact and select only a pattern supported by more than one entry.
parts.correct_explanation: Entries 2 and 6 show a repeated tendency to extend limited evidence into universal conclusions, which directly damages accuracy.

parts.prompt: Which correction routine best targets Sam's comma-splice pattern?

options.text: Circle every long word and replace it with a rarer synonym.
At each comma, check whether both sides could stand as complete sentences; if they can, use a full stop, semicolon or suitable conjunction, then reread the meaning.
Delete every comma from the response.
Write ‘be more careful’ in the margin and make no fresh attempt.

choice_rationales.A: Word rarity does not test sentence boundaries and may damage precision.
choice_rationales.B: The routine supplies a trigger, a clause test, valid correction choices and a meaning check.
choice_rationales.C: Many commas are correct; removing them all replaces one error with others.
choice_rationales.D: The instruction is vague and includes neither a check nor a retest.

parts.hint: The routine should tell Sam what to notice, what question to ask and what valid repair to make.
parts.correct_explanation: A short clause test turns the logged pattern into an action Sam can repeat on a new sentence.

parts.prompt: Which check best targets the unsupported-absolute pattern?

options.text: Underline every adjective, even when it does not affect the claim.
Find words such as every, all, always, never and proves; compare each claim with the measured group, time and outcome, then narrow any claim that travels beyond the evidence.
Add ‘definitely’ before each conclusion to make it sound certain.
Avoid reporting any result so that no conclusion can be questioned.

choice_rationales.A: The problem is evidence scope, not adjectives as a whole.
choice_rationales.B: The trigger words and boundary comparison directly test whether the conclusion exceeds the evidence.
choice_rationales.C: Extra certainty intensifies rather than corrects the pattern.
choice_rationales.D: The learner should report bounded results, not remove relevant evidence.

parts.hint: Use a visible language trigger and compare the claim with the exact limits of the evidence.
parts.correct_explanation: The scope check catches absolute wording and replaces it with a conclusion limited to what was actually observed.

parts.prompt: Which one-week plan would make Sam's error log most useful?

options.text: Copy all eight corrected answers once, mark every pattern as solved and discard the dates.

Keep comma splices and unsupported absolutes as the two active patterns; attach the clause-boundary and evidence-scope checks; complete fresh editing and composition items; record whether each error was avoided, self-corrected or found only after feedback; then review several later attempts before retiring either pattern.
Track all possible English errors at once and use ‘try harder’ as the correction routine for each.
Practise only the single preposition from entry 5 because the most recent-looking word-level error should replace all repeated patterns.

choice_rationales.A: Copying corrected answers does not demonstrate transfer, and removing dates destroys evidence of recurrence.
choice_rationales.B: The plan limits attention, links each pattern to an actionable check, uses fresh tasks and records the degree of independent control over time.
choice_rationales.C: Too many simultaneous priorities and a vague routine make progress difficult to practise or measure.
choice_rationales.D: A single word-level slip does not outweigh the repeated high-impact patterns.

parts.hint: Choose the plan with two priorities, specific checks, fresh retests and evidence collected over time.
parts.correct_explanation: A personal error log is a changing practice tool: it selects a small evidence-based target, guides action and requires successful transfer before retirement.
